title: The Blackthorn Bargain
objective: Inciting incident: Edric accepts the witches’ stolen authority, evidence, and blackthorn token, beginning the chain of choices through which his legitimate grievance will be reshaped into apparent fate and his destruction.
summary: Edric takes the witches’ stolen royal seal, incriminating ledger, and blackthorn token and turns toward court, beginning the chain of choices by which Huldah, Ysop, and Merrin will turn his just grievance into the appearance of fate and engineer his destruction.
prose_content:
### Scene 1: The Blackthorn Bargain

Rain had followed Edric from the eastern road and found Wyrmwood’s graves first. At dusk, black water showed between the tussocks, and rain silvered the bent grass. The village should have smelled of peat smoke and wet wool. Instead, lime and rot had settled over the houses, sharp enough to taste on the back of his tongue.

Red cloth marked the doors of infected houses. Two had been nailed shut from outside, and a burial cart turned at the crossroad with its load hidden beneath oiled canvas. No one rang the plague bell. Its rope had been cut, perhaps so sickness would not mistake a summons for a cure.

His roan picked its way through the mud, hooves slipping against loose stone. The sword at Edric’s left thigh kept striking his boot. Ten days earlier, a clerk in the war ministry had scraped Captain from his command tablet and pressed King Alaric’s revocation into the old space beside his name. The tablet still hung inside his coat, its brass edge pressing a bruise into his ribs. He had not returned it. Neither had he returned the dead.

At least, not the ones owed burial.

He had come to Wyrmwood because its levy had supplied half his brigade and its dead had supplied most of his last march. The war ledger claimed every man had been paid in full. The families he had left behind knew coin, not typography. When Edric demanded a count, the king had answered by taking his rank.

Names filled the crossroad board beneath its rotting hood. More likely a burial roll. Names belonged now to whichever ledger the living feared to open.

An old woman stood beyond the fence with two companions. Rain had pasted white hair to her temples. The younger woman beside her kept working a copper wire around the gate latch, stripping green metal from her fingers. The third carried a ledger case under one arm and watched Edric with the patience of a man waiting for a sum to balance.

> “Captain Vane,” the old woman said.

> “There is no longer a Captain Vane,” Edric said.

> “The moor remembers one.”

> “The moor remembers corpses.”

> “It remembers who denied them their pay.”

His hand rested near his sword, not drawing, only measuring. Two roads met at the gate. One led back toward the burial cart. The other crossed open ground toward the abandoned tithe house.

> “I came for my dead,” he said. “Not for prophecy.”

> “They are not moving,” Huldah said. “It may be for that reason they need you.”

He dismounted. The rain struck the crown of his command tablet where it hung beneath his coat. Huldah watched, but said nothing. The woman called Ysop opened the gate at last, and Merrin carried the ledger case inside.

The tithe house had one door, one shuttered window, and a cellar hatch secured by a new lock. Edric marked all three before stepping inside. Ysop shut the door behind him and returned to her copper wire. Whatever she had repaired, the latch no longer needed the wall to help it.

Wet ash, vinegar, and iron gall filled the room. Two long tables had been pushed together. Burial slips covered one end, their names fading beneath rain spots. At the other lay military payrolls bound in grey file.

> “The count is already here,” Merrin said.

Huldah left the explanation to him.

Merrin opened the nearest ledger. The wet leather resisted, then gave with a soft tear. His finger moved down a column until it stopped.

*VANE’S BRIGADE, EASTERN MARCH: PAY DISCHARGED IN FULL.*

Edric’s fingers pressed the table hard enough to whiten the old sword blister across his palm. Some names belonged to men he had carried from the final march. Men whose boots he had wrapped before the roads froze. Men whose last words had been requests for water, coin, or enough time to reach home.

Across the table, a burial roll carried several of the same names.

> “The crown buried what it would not pay,” Huldah said.

> “The king may know nothing of this.”

> “Then the king has never opened the correct book.”

Merrin turned the ledger. A transfer order crossed the final payment, every blank filled in a narrow official hand. Chancellor Merea’s cipher closed the record like a lock with no visible key.

> “Merea authorized the transfer,” Edric said.

> “Merea’s cipher did.”

> “That is not an answer.”

> “It is the answer available until someone needs a better one.”

Merrin set a square of black wool on the table. Beneath it lay an iron seal no longer than his palm. He turned the handle, and a crowned wolf emerged in reverse.

Edric knew the device. Every quartermaster in the eastern campaign had received orders stamped with that mark.

> “The King’s Lesser Seal,” Huldah said. “Taken from the records vault beneath Merea’s keeping.”

> “You stole it from the Chancellor.”

> “We stole it from a room.”

> “The distinction will matter when Merea discovers the theft.”

> “Not as much as discovering what his cipher authorized.”

Ysop abandoned the latch and spread a narrow floor plan across the payrolls. Four rooms surrounded a hall marked in charcoal.

> “A complaint passed through the ministry will be answered by the ministry,” she said. “The same complaint placed before the king cannot return to anonymity.”

> “You have arranged an audience.”

> “I have arranged for an audience to become inconvenient.”

Edric looked from the floor plan to the stolen seal.

> “Merea will see it.”

> “He will.”

> “Will he help us?”

> “He will defend his office first. Justice may follow if it learns to walk quietly.”

Merrin laid a narrower register beside the ledger. Names filled its columns, followed by trades, wounds, and places of residence. Several men Edric knew were listed there. Others belonged to no company he had commanded.

> “Witnesses,” Merrin said.

Edric touched one unfamiliar name.

> “Where is this man?”

> “His location has not yet become useful.”

> “You mean you have not found him.”

> “I mean his whereabouts will not bear close inquiry.”

Edric flattened the page with two fingers.

> “You mean you mean to invent him.”

> “Memory can be helped to remember what a man needed.”

> “That is false witness.”

> “That is witness under pressure.”

> “It is testimony bought with another man’s neck.”

Huldah watched him without defending either principle.

> “A fact does not become less true because the king refuses it.”

> “Neither does a man become less guilty for being useful.”

> “No,” Huldah said. “But the guilty are easier to reach.”

Edric’s thumb remained on the open register. He should have pushed it back. Instead, he withdrew his hand, and Merrin closed the book between them.

No oath passed between them. Agreement did not require one.

Ysop returned to her floor plan and indicated a chamber above the hall.

> “On the ninth day, the king will dine beneath a roof with his council,” she said. “There will be an eclipse.”

> “I know what an eclipse is.”

> “So does every court. The difference is what they are prepared to call a sign.”

> “You expect Merea to grant me leave to enter.”

> “I expect him to believe granting it was his idea.”

> “And if he remembers he never gave the invitation?”

> “By then, witnesses will remember it for him.”

Edric looked at the closed register.

> “You expect me to blame the moor when this fails.”

> “I expect men to blame the road once it becomes inconvenient.”

> “I arranged none of it.”

> “Not yet,” Huldah said.

She placed the last object in the center of the table.

The blackthorn token was formed as a ring. Pale cuts showed where branches had been trimmed, and one thorn curved inward. Rainwater beaded along its dark grain. It smelled of bitter bark, cleaner than anything else in the room.

> “Does it compel me?” Edric said.

> “No,” Huldah said. “It remembers.”

> “Remembers what?”

> “What you do.”

The answer was not enough to make it safe. It was precise enough to make refusal expensive.

Huldah placed two fingers beside the token without touching it.

> “Take the ledger. Take the Lesser Seal. Go to Merea, and let him discover whether the hand behind the theft is his enemy or himself. Keep our names from the king until the matter is answered.”

> “If it is never answered?”

> “Then what you have done will remain.”

> “That is not a term. That is an omen.”

> “Terms are what men use to make consequences look like furniture.”

Edric reached for the ring. The inward thorn found the groove between his fingers and pressed there as he lifted it.

> “If I accept your terms, the moor keeps my name.”

> “The moor keeps every name given to it,” Huldah said. “It does not always return one.”

> “That is not reassuring.”

> “The dead do not demand reassurance. They ask for a grave.”

Edric slid the blackthorn onto his little finger. It fit without pinching. He pulled once, and the ring resisted only so much as wet wood could be expected to resist. The inward thorn settled over his pulse, keeping time with blood already beginning to move faster.

> “I agree to your secrecy,” he said. “Until the ledger is answered.”

Huldah inclined her head.

Merrin wrapped the Lesser Seal in oilcloth and gave it to him. Edric placed it inside his coat, where the revocation tablet pressed against his ribs. The lesser mark and the greater one now shared the same coat, one issuing commands and one erasing the man who had carried them.

The ledger went into his saddlebag. He folded the stolen warrant inside it, between the lists of dead and living. None of the paper was clean. This made the evidence easier to believe.

> “Captain Vane,” Huldah said as he reached the door.

Edric stopped.

> “Edric Vane,” he said.

Huldah offered no correction.

Outside, the burial cart had reached the far end of the village. Its wheels ground black furrows into the road. The roan lowered its head toward the smell, and Edric tightened the reins until the horse’s teeth showed.

He looked back once. Through the open doorway, he saw Merrin bend over a clean page. Ysop’s green-stained fingers worked at the latch. Huldah stood between them, watching neither the road nor the ledger.

The Lesser Seal was stolen. His veterans had been robbed. Both facts remained true, but only one of them fit beneath Edric’s coat.

He fastened it there anyway.

At the crossroad, he turned south toward the king’s court. The blackthorn settled more securely over his pulse, and Edric took the motion for a yes.
cliffhanger: The blackthorn keeps time with Edric’s pulse as he takes the road to Merea and the eclipse banquet, but will he recognize the witches’ engineered events before they become the choices by which he destroys himself?
continuity_notes: The POV remains close third fixed on Edric Vane.
Edric is returning from the eastern war and has been formally stripped of his captain’s rank by King Alaric after demanding an accounting of unpaid veteran wages.
Wyrmwood is devastated by plague; infected houses are marked, burial rolls are being maintained, and many roads and buildings stand empty.
Edric’s brigade was recorded as fully paid, but the money and veterans’ families received neither, and the transfers bear Chancellor Merea’s cipher without proving Merea personally ordered the theft.
The witches provide Edric with evidence of the corrupt transfers and the stolen King’s Lesser Seal, which is distinct from King Alaric’s personal signet.
The bargain requires secrecy regarding Huldah, Ysop, and Merrin while Edric pursues the matter at court.
Huldah frames Edric’s choices as fate, Ysop plans access to the eclipse banquet, and Merrin supplies or engineers witnesses whose reliability depends on pressure and false memory.
Edric deliberately takes the blackthorn token, a close-fitting thorn ring, and chooses to return toward the king’s court with the stolen seal and ledger.
The token’s supernatural nature remains ambiguous; no actual compulsion or independent voice is yet confirmed.
